summary: A 1970 note commenting on the Meyer proposal, referring to protocol ideas by another author in the group. It adds feedback from RAND.

plainLanguage.summary: More feedback on someone's idea, sent in by people at another lab.

questions: what did rand say about meyer proposal
when did rand endorse the ncp protocol
subtitle: RAND Corporation's feedback supporting the Meyer proposal with some proposed modifications

tldr.problem: The Meyer proposal is more acceptable than previous complex proposals, but some design choices in RFC 46 and RFC 49 need clarification or modification.
tldr.mechanism: Harslem and Heafner endorse the Meyer proposal's simplicity and extensibility. They support keeping dynamic reconnection for later, including the INT command, adding instance tags for process distinction, standardizing ASCII for teletype communication, and supporting the proposed UCC protocol for login.
tldr.outcome: This feedback from RAND reinforces consensus on the basic protocol design, clearing the way for formal specification and implementation.

today: RFC 50 represents institutional buy-in from a major research center, reinforcing the Meyer proposal's viability. The RAND endorsement helped build consensus for what would become the first ARPANET host protocol.

sections.title: Support for Meyer's Approach
sections.content: Harslem and Heafner from the RAND Corporation find the Meyer proposal to be the most acceptable proposal to date, precisely because it is simple, sufficient for planned network uses, easy to implement, and extensible. They recognize that it does not encompass every suggested feature, but they argue that the missing features are not worth delaying the specification. This perspective proves crucial: they validate the design philosophy that a good initial standard beats a perfect one that takes years to negotiate.
sections.plainLanguage: RAND agrees that Meyer's simple proposal is better than trying to include everything, even if some features are left out.

sections.title: Agreed Design Decisions
sections.content: Harslem and Heafner agree on several key points from the debate: dynamic reconnection should wait for later implementations (not in the initial protocol), the INT interrupt command is valuable and easy to implement, and they support including instance tags in socket identifiers to distinguish multiple processes. Notably, they support standardizing on a character set (ASCII is their preference, matching the IMP standard) for teletype-to-foreign-monitor communication. They endorse the UCC protocol proposal, noting that users should not need to know remote socket codes. They also prefer the BLK and RSM commands for flow control, which do not impede later multiplexing of sockets over a single link.
sections.plainLanguage: They agree on keeping the protocol simple now, adding features later, supporting INT commands, using ASCII for text, and having a standard login protocol.

sections.title: Installation-Specific Implementation
sections.content: The RFC includes a note that some design choices are installation-dependent. Specifically, they mention that UCC's ability to close connections of dead processes can vary depending on how each site's operating system notifies the NCP of process failures. At RAND, the NCP is notified directly through the software interface used by all processes. This acknowledgment shows the authors' understanding that different computer systems will implement the protocol differently, as long as the external behavior (the protocol itself) remains compatible.
sections.plainLanguage: Different computers might build the protocol differently on the inside, as long as the network connections work the same way.
